```markdown
# Batch Tracking: Mash Day to Bottle

## Intent and why
The brewery needs to trace any bottle back to the ingredients that went
into it. A bottle's label leads to its batch, and the batch leads to the
lot number of every malt and hop sack used in it. This is the record you
reach for when a customer, an inspector, or a supplier asks "what's in
this bottle, and where did it come from?"

## Goals
- Record each batch from mash day through bottling.
- Record the lot number of every malt and hop sack that goes into a batch.
- Capture sack lot numbers by scanning when the sack is opened, not by
  typing, because the brewers' hands are usually wet.
- At bottling, print labels that carry the batch number and the bottling
  date.
- From a batch number on a bottle, show the batch and every sack lot in it.

## Non-goals
- Inventory or stock levels of malt and hops.
- Recipes, brew-day measurements (gravity, temperatures), or fermentation
  logs.
- Tracing beyond the sack lot number (for example, the supplier's own
  records).
- Changes to the existing taproom tab features.

## Anti-goals (failure even if it technically works)
- Brewers have to type lot numbers by hand on the brew floor.
- A bottled batch exists with no sack lots recorded and nobody notices.
- Lookup from a bottle takes more than a minute or needs someone who
  knows SQL.

## Constraints
- Runs on the existing Raspberry Pi in the office, alongside the taproom
  app.
- Existing stack: Flask and SQLite. Build on it.
- The label printer used at bottling is already in place.

## Approaches
1. **Extend the existing Flask app** with batch-tracking tables and pages.
   One app, one database, one thing to back up. Risk: the taproom and
   brewing parts share a codebase, so keep the new code in its own module.
2. **A separate small app on the same Pi.** Clean separation, but a
   second service to run, update, and back up, for no gain at this size.
3. **Off-the-shelf brewery software or a spreadsheet.** No build, but
   spreadsheets don't scan and print well, and brewery suites bring
   far more than this needs plus a subscription.

**Pick (my call):** 1, extend the existing app, in its own module.

## The how, as decided
- A batch runs from mash day to bottling and has a batch number.
- Each malt or hop sack's lot number is printed on the sack and is
  scanned when the sack is opened, recording it against the batch.
- At bottling, each label gets the batch number and bottling date.

## My calls (for review)
- **Scanner:** a USB or Bluetooth barcode scanner that acts as a keyboard,
  so scanning into a page's input field needs no special drivers. If the
  sack lot numbers aren't barcoded, the builder should flag it before
  starting.
- **Batch number format:** `YYYY-NNN` (year plus running count), assigned
  automatically on mash day. Short enough to print and read off a label.
- **Reverse lookup:** from a sack lot number, list every batch that used
  it, for the case where a supplier recalls a lot. Same data, one extra
  page.
- **Guard:** the bottling step warns if a batch has no malt or no hop
  lots recorded.
- **Corrections:** a mis-scanned lot can be removed from a batch before
  bottling; after bottling, the record is read-only.

## Units
- **Data (`batches`, `sack_lots`, `batch_sack_lots`)**: the batch record,
  each scanned lot (type: malt/hop, lot number, scanned-at), and the link
  between them. Own SQLite tables in the existing database.
- **Brew-floor pages**: start a batch; scan sacks into the open batch;
  remove a mis-scan. Large controls, usable with wet hands.
- **Bottling**: close the batch with a bottling date and send label jobs
  to the existing printer.
- **Lookup pages**: batch number → batch and lots; lot number → batches.

## Left to the builder
- How to talk to the existing label printer (driver, label template
  layout) after checking its model.
- Page layout and styling, following the taproom app's conventions.
- Migration approach for the new tables.
```

Understood. Writing it up now, at `specs/batch-tracking.md`.

One call you didn't make, so you know: I'm building this into your existing taproom app on the Pi, in its own section, rather than as a separate program or off-the-shelf brewery software. One app means one thing to run and back up. A few other things I filled in are listed at the end of the doc under "My calls," like the batch number format and a lookup from a sack lot to every batch that used it, for supplier recalls.

A reviewer is reading it as a builder would before I hand it over. If they turn up anything only you can answer, I'll bring it back in one short message. Otherwise the next thing you'll see is the finished doc to review.
